name: シャーク コーヒー (SHARK COFFEE) (Shark Coffee)

claims.text: FindMeGlutenFree listing states the establishment is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for those with celiac disease; recommends contacting the establishment directly about safety precautions.

Menu and directory data show dairy items (Greek yogurt; cafe latte with dairy option, oat/rice/almond only as +charge alternatives), confirming the menu is not exclusively vegan and not a controlled allergen-free environment.

All corroborating sources describe GF menu variety ('so many GF and vegan options,' 'wonderful assortment') but none document cross-contamination handling, a dedicated fryer, or staff allergen training — no celiac-grade handling evidence exists.
Sweets and food are curated by an organic consultant specifically for gluten-free, vegan, and additive-free needs.
Food menu includes gluten-free cakes, pizza, hot dogs, curry bread, and rice-flour carrot cake.
Coffee and most drinks (including chai and kombucha) are made from 100% organic ingredients, with organic plant-milk options for lattes.

name: スパイスカリー はちわん 神保町店 (Spice Curry Hachiwan (Jimbocho))

claims.text: Shop concept and all media coverage confirm the curry is built on mackerel (鯖) and bonito (かつお) dashi plus miso — the GF story is only about omitting the flour roux, and says nothing about soy sauce, which in Japanese cooking overwhelmingly contains wheat and is unconfirmed here.

The offering includes a self-serve 副菜ビュッフェ (side-dish buffet: achar pickles, vegetables, soup, and 'spicy chicken'), an inherent cross-contamination vector whose items are not documented as wheat-free; 'spicy chicken' may be fried/karaage.

No FindMeGlutenFree or HappyCow celiac review of Hachiwan Jimbocho exists; searches for glutened/negative celiac reports returned nothing — consistent with a Nov-2025 opening and no independent celiac verification of handling rather than proven safety.

The only explicit GF/no-wheat-flour claim originates from the shop's own site; media pieces repeat that concept, so there are not two INDEPENDENT sources of real GF handling as required for a 'high' rating.
The curry base is made without wheat flour, using vegetable, spice, and Japanese dashi umami instead of a flour roux — the shop's stated central concept.
No cross-contamination policy, dedicated equipment, or gluten-free certification is published by the shop in any source found.
Core products — tofu, fresh yuba, and edamame tofu — are made from 100% domestic soybeans and natural nigari with no listed animal-derived dashi or additives.

name: WE ARE THE FARM 渋谷 (We Are The Farm Shibuya)

claims.text: Restaurant offers only a limited-quantity gluten-free/vegan/low-sugar tart as a specifically labeled GF item; no statement found that the broader menu, sauces, or fryer are gluten-free or cross-contamination controlled.
Regular menu contains many animal-based items, so the vegan course is recommended to be reserved in advance rather than ordered ad hoc from the standard menu.
A hot-pot dish combines a vegetable-scrap "veggie broth" with Japanese dashi, which commonly includes bonito (katsuobushi) unless a plant-based dashi is specifically requested.
All vegetables are grown on the group's own organic farm in Sakura, Chiba, without pesticides or chemical fertilizers, and are marketed as harvested and delivered fresh each morning.

name: With Green 道玄坂通店 (WithGreen Shibuya Dogenzaka-dori)

claims.text: The chain's allergen chart flags wheat, soy, and apple as allergens present in the finishing sauces/dressings, and notes possible cross-contamination between menu items; customers are advised to check with in-store staff for specifics.
Several of the chain's dressings are soy/wheat-based finishing sauces (後かけのタレ) that are called out specifically as containing wheat and soy allergens.

At least one dressing (a lemon-based dressing) is labeled vegetarian/vegan-compatible on the chain's menu at other WithGreen branches (Kagurazaka, Aoyama); it is not confirmed whether this exact labeling is posted at the Dogenzaka-dori branch.
The chain directs customers with allergen concerns, including questions about honey use and potential cross-contamination, to ask in-store staff directly rather than relying solely on printed charts.
Salads are built to order from a wide choice of over 10 dressings and toppings, using domestically grown Japanese vegetables.

name: ウッドベリー ベーカリー（WOODBERRY BAKERY） (Woodberry Bakery)

claims.text: Gluten-free options are prepared in a shared bakery environment and are not recommended for highly sensitive celiacs.

Reviewers describe lots of clearly labeled vegan pastries throughout the case, a full coffee selection with non-dairy milk options, and staff willing to pack items into customers' own containers on request.
A Japanese food blogger noted the vegan bread and pastries had good texture and didn't feel heavy in the stomach after eating.
No soy sauce information found in any source; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and is common in café kitchens. Assume wheat-containing soy sauce unless confirmed otherwise.

name: ガネーシャダイニング (Ganesha Dining)

claims.text: No information found about dedicated preparation surfaces or separate utensils for gluten-free dishes. Naan is baked in a tandoor oven and prepared with wheat dough; shared kitchen risk cannot be excluded.
Soy sauce does not appear to be used in the standard Indian/Nepalese curry preparations here, but no allergen chart has been published so this cannot be confirmed.
Dairy (butter, cream, paneer) is used extensively in several curries. Whether plant-based curries share cooking vessels with dairy-based ones is unknown; staff should be asked.
Tabelog notes 'allergy information available' but no published allergen matrix was found during research. Recommend asking staff directly in Japanese.
Multiple plant-based curry options (vegetable, chickpea, lentil, eggplant-potato) are standard menu items, not special requests, making vegetarian ordering straightforward.
